title: Arithmetic definability: enumerable sets and quantifiers
summary: An enumerable set is exactly a set described in arithmetic by an unbounded search followed by a bounded check.
abstract: A successful computation has a finite record, so recognizing an input can be viewed as searching for a record that passes a terminating check. Arithmetic formulas can express exactly this kind of search. Over the ordinary natural numbers, a set is computably enumerable precisely when membership can be stated by choosing finitely many numerical witnesses and checking a bounded arithmetic condition. Negating a description of this form gives a definition of a set whose nonmembers can be recognized. A set with both kinds of description is decidable, and every decidable set has both. The halting set illustrates why an arithmetic definition need not give a decision procedure. Requiring a program to halt on every input introduces another quantifier: each input must have its own successful computation record.
